newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu-Arafat meeting seen calming investors.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu-Arafat meeting seen calming investors.

text.p: The handshake last week between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat sent a positive signal to international investors, a prominent British businessman on Sunday.

"The bombings (in Israel), the assassination of (former prime minister Yitzhak Rabin) and the radical change of the elections created uncertainty in Israel and fears about the continuation of the peace process," Lord Young told Reuters.
"Now, after the handshake, enthusiasm (among investors) is building up though maybe not as much as it was a year ago. People are seeing that the situation is settling down."
Hardliner Netanyahu, who ousted Labour leader Shimon Peres in May 29 elections, held a landmark summit with Arafat on Wednesday.

Young, chairman of investment bank Young Associates Ltd and former chairman of Cable & Wireless, said Netanyahu's planned visit to Britain at the end of the month would further calm fears on the progress of peace.
He said investors in Europe are still unaware of how big Israel's economy is, but to continue to grow Israel needed to undertake economic reforms.
"There is more of a chance now for the economy to change because the prime minister is much keener on deregulation and privatisation," he said.
As Minister of Trade and Industry Young was instrumental in privatising British companies under former prime minister Margaret Thatcher.
Young is also the representative of British Gas in Israel. He said the British company was interested in taking part in the tender for a proposed Israel-Egyptian natural gas pipeline.
Young was participating in a seminar for a British trade mission led by James Clappison, Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for the Environment.

Wavell Magor, first commercial secretary at the British Embassy in Tel Aviv, said British businessmen had not been deterred by the change in Israel's government, adding that the embassy was expecting 12 trade missions to Israel next year.
"It is business as usual," he said.
